newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Jobs, rights top EU treaty draft.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Jobs, rights top EU treaty draft.

text.p: The European Union unveiled a draft treaty on Thursday making job creation a prime focus of EU policy and offering its citizens a broad range of freedoms in a secure and just continent.

It called for the bloc to streamline its decision making and speak with a more forceful voice on the world stage, and proposed a framework allowing the EU's keenest integrationists to move ahead of others if they wish.

The draft, prepared by the Dutch presidency for EU leaders at a summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday, is the culmination of 15 months of negotiation in part designed to prepare the bloc for enlargement into eastern Europe.
Leaders are expected to emphasise the inclusion of an Employment Chapter in the treaty, initially proposed by the Nordic countries but now pushed forcefully by France's new Socialist government.

It makes job creation a formal goal of the EU and creates mechanisms for discussing employment policy between member states. But it offers no financial programmes for boosting jobs bar some for the exchange of information and pilot projects.
In another move to court citizens and bring them closer to the Union, the draft seeks to beef up efforts by the EU to crack down on organised crime.
It also promises protection against discrimination on grounds of sex, racial and ethnic origin, religion and belief, disability, age, or sexual orientation.

Among its other proposals -- all subject to veto by any EU member state at the summit -- is the integration of the Schengen border-free pact into the bloc, lifting borders across what the treaty draft calls an area of freedom, security and justice.
Britain and Ireland would be given an opt-out from the Schengen provisions and be allowed to keep their frontier checks.
The Dutch draft also calls for the eventual incorporation of the Western European Union grouping into the bloc as the EU's defence arm.
Although the draft gives no date for this to happen, the idea is expected to be fought by Britain, Denmark and the EU's neutrals, Ireland, Austria, Finland and Sweden.
Moves by France and Germany to limit the number of EU commissioners, now 20, have been scaled back.

The draft implies that big countries will give up one of their two commissioners when the EU enlarges by between two and six countries and calls for a review of the issue when the number of EU countries reaches 20.
Small countries had vehemently fought for the right to retain their commissioner, seen as the guarantor of their voices in the bloc.
In exchange, however, the draft says larger countries should be given more power in decision making when ministers meet.

Majority voting -- once a major headache for negotiators because of the former British Conservative government's opposition to losing its veto -- would be extended in non-sensitive areas such as research.
